content:
Earlier this year, Apple decided to completely discontinue its Pro Display XDR. Although it was an outstanding hardware product, it hadn't been updated for years and still retailed for over US$6,000. Apple's new display lineup consists of the Studio Display and the all-new Studio Display XDR—both excellent in their own right, but both now only available as 27-inch 5K displays. The XDR starts at a hefty US$3,299 and can be configured up to US$3,600 before tax. This has left a gap in the market, waiting for someone to release a larger Retina-class display for Mac users—and that's exactly where the brand-new Meirro Pro comes in. The Meirro Pro is a 32-inch 6K display, built entirely from aluminium, supporting single-cable connection, with an adjustable stand, all for just US$1,199. I've been using it as my primary display, and although Meirro made some trade-offs to hit that price point, it might be the most compelling Studio Display alternative to date. Here's everything you need to know.

Be sure to check out our hands-on Meirro Pro video to see the product firsthand!

Design & Specifications

First and foremost, what's most striking is how closely it resembles the existing Apple Studio Display in appearance. This monitor fits naturally and beautifully into any Apple-centric setup. It's constructed from fully CNC-machined aluminium with a matching adjustable stand, and it feels exceptionally premium. The build quality inspires tremendous confidence in any setup. Most non-Apple displays use plastic enclosures, and the stands are usually flimsier than ideal, but there's not a trace of plastic anywhere in the Meirro Pro's construction.

Unboxing and setup are also refreshingly simple. You simply attach the base to the stand, then secure the stand to the back of the display, plug in the power, and you're up and running. The monitor design is exceptionally minimalist, with no buttons whatsoever—and best of all, the power supply is built into the display itself. So there's no bulky power brick dangling from your power cable, keeping your setup extremely clean. The monitor comes with both an adjustable stand and a VESA mount included in the box at no extra cost. So yes, it's a very Apple-esque design and aesthetic, which suits me perfectly.

But at the end of the day, how does the display itself perform? As I mentioned at the outset, this is a true 6K panel. It's a 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel with a resolution of 6144 × 3456, equivalent to 224 ppi, delivering Retina-class clarity. Here are the key specs:

  • 32-inch Nano IPS Black panel
  • 6144 × 3456 resolution
  • 224 PPI
  • 60Hz refresh rate
  • 2,000:1 contrast ratio
  • 10-bit colour supporting over 1.07 billion colours
  • 98% DCI-P3 colour gamut coverage
  • 99.5% Adobe RGB colour gamut coverage
  • Typical brightness of 450 nits, HDR peak brightness of 750 nits

This panel also comes with a glossy anti-reflective coating as the only display option. While I'd also love to have a matte option available, the glossy coating still looks excellent even in a room with plenty of windows.

Ports & Accessories

Similar to Apple's display offerings, the Meirro Pro keeps things minimalist, offering only five USB-C ports on the back for input and output. One of these serves as the primary upstream port, supporting DisplayPort 2.1, up to 80Gbps bandwidth, and up to 96W of power delivery to keep your MacBook charged. So a single cable handles the 6K video signal. The other four USB-C ports are downstream ports, but since they're USB 2.0, data transfer speeds are rather limited. However, they're perfectly adequate for webcams, speakers, and other peripherals.

Since the Meirro Pro has no buttons whatsoever—not even a power button—a remote control that looks remarkably similar to the previous-generation Apple TV remote is included in the box. This remote has a power button and can access the display's system settings when needed.

My Experience & Setup

I've been using the Meirro Pro as my sole primary display in my desk setup, and the experience has been outstanding. The combination of a 32-inch screen size and 6K resolution gives me the practical workspace and pixel density I'd expect from a high-end Mac display.

My setup is straightforward. I frequently use external SSDs and prefer the Satechi Thunderbolt hub, so I connect the display through that hub. I run a Thunderbolt cable from the display to the hub, then another Thunderbolt cable from the hub to my MacBook Pro. Everything works as expected.

I tested this display with all my usual workflows, and it handled everything with ease. I tested it with Final Cut Pro, including working on timelines and organising all my media files, and the extra screen real estate was genuinely helpful. A significant portion of my daily work involves research, requiring numerous tabs and windows open simultaneously; the extra pixel density makes it feel larger than a mere 32-inch display. The most important characteristic of this monitor is its 224 PPI, which allows macOS and even iPadOS to scale exactly as Apple intended.

Finally, I want to mention that the build quality genuinely helps reduce wobble. Most displays of this kind wobble when you type at your desk, especially if you're using a sit-stand desk like I am. So the combination of build materials and a sturdy stand effectively mitigates the wobble issue. Therefore, whether on paper or in real-world use, the Meirro Pro makes a compelling case as a Studio Display alternative. But at this price point, there are still some trade-offs worth discussing.

The Trade-offs

Again, a 32-inch 6K display made of CNC aluminium for under US$1,200 sounds almost too good to be true. Meirro had to make some decisions to bring the price down to this level. Since most potential buyers will compare it to the Studio Display, it's worth noting the omitted features. The Meirro Pro does not include or support the following:

  • No built-in webcam
  • No speakers
  • No microphone
  • No daisy-chaining support

Personally, these omissions are worth the cost savings, as I already own external webcams and speakers. The lack of a microphone isn't an issue either, since I use AirPods or a Shure microphone when needed. But I want to flag these caveats so anyone considering this display knows what to expect.

The final trade-off I noticed is the speed of the USB-C ports on the back of the display. Apple's Studio Display offers a total of four USB-C ports, two of which are Thunderbolt and the other two are USB 3.0 speed. The Meirro Pro does offer more USB-C ports, but only one is Thunderbolt—the remaining four are slower USB 2.0. For me this isn't a major issue since I have a Satechi Thunderbolt dock, but I can understand how other users might need faster ports.

But even with these trade-offs in mind, I still think this is an easier recommendation than Apple's Studio Display, because the value the Meirro Pro delivers is simply too high.

Pricing & Availability

The Meirro Pro has a regular retail price of US$1,299 and is currently available for pre-order at US$1,199, with shipping expected to begin on August 1st. Technically, you can opt out of the stand and save US$50 (if you already have a monitor arm), bringing the total down to US$1,149. The US$1,199 price includes the following:

  • Meirro Pro display
  • Aluminium stand
  • VESA mount
  • USB-C cable
  • Power cable
  • Remote control

Wrap-up

The Meirro Pro is the best true Studio Display alternative I've tested. At US$1,199, you get a 32-inch 6K display with Retina-class clarity, a glossy Nano IPS Black panel, all-aluminium construction, single-cable Mac connectivity, an adjustable stand, and a VESA mount. If you want Apple's most complete all-in-one desktop experience, the Studio Display still has its merits, but if you already have some external accessories and truly value screen size, resolution, build quality, and value for money, the Meirro Pro is an easy recommendation.

What do you think? Would you consider this display? Do you already own a Studio Display? Will you miss the Pro Display XDR? I'd love to hear your thoughts. Again, be sure to watch our video to see it in action!
